title: Phone Bans Are a Good Thing…
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau argues that school phone bans are right policy but that lockable pouches—currently the most commercially visible implementation—may be the wrong tool, because the phone's mere physical proximity continues to occupy cognitive bandwidth even when locked. A 2026 NBER study on lockable pouch adoption found in-class phone use fell from 61% to 13%, but standardized test scores showed effects 'consistently close to zero,' with first-year increases in disciplinary incidents and slight wellbeing dips. Didau contextualizes this against Ward et al.'s 2017 'brain drain' research, which showed cognitive performance degrades based on smartphone proximity—not just active use—meaning pouches solve the behavioral problem while leaving the psychological problem intact. He identifies three cheaper alternatives ranked by effectiveness: phones left at home (culturally clearest), phones switched off in bags with immediate confiscation if seen or heard, and tutor-time collection with end-of-day return. His deeper argument is that pouches convert a cultural challenge into a procurement decision, with the vendor (Yondr) supplying data and framing that subtly colonizes public education policy through commercial convenience, and that the ideal phone ban is invisible—phones simply absent from students' attentional field rather than locked on their person all day.
points: The NBER study found lockable pouches reduced in-class phone use from 61% to 13% but produced near-zero effects on test scores, attendance, and bullying—suggesting pouch-based bans address the behavioral use problem but not the underlying attention-disruption problem.

Ward et al.'s 'brain drain' research found cognitive performance correlates with phone location (out of room > bag > desk) regardless of whether the phone is on or off—meaning pouches, which keep phones on students' bodies, may leave the core cognitive cost intact.

Phone pouch companies shift the school's policy question from 'how do we create a phone-free culture?' to 'should we buy this product?'—a commercial capture of public policy that leaders should name explicitly when evaluating implementation options.

Three alternatives with descending cultural effectiveness: phones left at home (clearest signal, requires winning the parental argument), phones off in bags with immediate confiscation (cheap but culture-dependent), tutor-time collection and return (best practical compromise for most schools).

A good phone policy reduces daily adult transactions; pouches risk increasing them by creating a new compliance economy of damaged, forgotten, or tampered devices that generate fresh disciplinary categories—exactly what the NBER paper's first-year incident spike reflects.
quotes: A phone-free school should begin with culture, not kit.

The pouch system bans phones from being used but encourages students to bring them to school. The school day is phone-free, except every student carries a locked phone around all day like a tiny imprisoned goblin of distraction. This isn't so much a ban as a compromise with a zip.
Corporate interests colonise public policy through convenience, visibility and our weakness for solutions that arrive pre-packaged.

The best phone bans are boring. Phones aren't seen, staff don't spend the day negotiating, students aren't invited into endless procedural theatre, and the rule is simple enough to become part of the weather of the school.

Schools are one of the few remaining places where adults can say to children: for a few hours, you don't have to be available to everyone else. You don't have to respond, perform, monitor your status, inspect your humiliations, defend your streaks or keep one eye on the latest tiny drama unfolding in a group chat named after something unprintable.
Phones out of sight is a start but phones out of reach is better and phones out of the room is better still. And, where possible, phones out of school is best.
